# Delta Air Lines and Fundación Patagonia Azul helped shape the next generation of Juan Fernández “Guardians of the Sea”


For the second consecutive year, Delta Air Lines supported marine conservation in Chile with an educational program that reached students in the archipelago, from nursery through the final year of high school, and provided teaching materials that now remain permanently on the island.


Staff Writer


Nov 24, 2026 4:30pm


Delta Air Lines renewed its commitment to Chile’s ocean and once again joined forces with Fundación Patagonia Azul, this time to support a new Marine Conservation Education Program for the Juan Fernández Archipelago. The initiative brought the island’s marine heritage into the classroom on an ongoing basis for the first time, as a complement to the formal school curriculum, and accompanied students from early childhood education through the end of high school.


“Chile is home to LATAM, our partner airline in South America, and over these four years of joint venture we have built a commitment here that goes beyond connecting destinations," said Soledad Lago Rodriguez, Communications Manager for Latin America at Delta Air Lines. " Supporting the protection of Chile’s ocean, now from the classrooms of Juan Fernández, is part of that commitment."

### **First Patagonia, then Juan Fernández**


The partnership began in 2025 in Chilean Patagonia. That year, Delta and Fundación Patagonia Azul supported the communities of the Pitipalena-Añihué Multiple-Use Coastal Marine Protected Area with cutting-edge technology and training to strengthen the monitoring and protection of their ecosystem. In the second year, the focus shifted to education, reaching the students growing up to safeguard one of the most valuable territories on the planet for biodiversity and marine conservation.


The timing was no coincidence. At the time, Juan Fernández was seeking to make history with the expansion of the Mar de Juan Fernández and Nazca-Desventuradas Marine Parks, aiming to protect a 337,230 km² sanctuary, similar in size to Germany. The idea for the initiative originated within the island’s own community of artisanal fishers. However, that biocultural heritage still had no place in the classroom. The enormous challenges of this island territory, including high teacher turnover, a lack of materials adapted to island life, and the absence of an educational repository on the island, had prevented environmental education initiatives from being sustained over time.


### **Learning from the ocean at every stage of school**


To help close that gap, the program was designed together with the community, with scientific grounding and collaboration, and offered learning experiences tailored to each educational level and deeply connected to the island. The youngest children, in nursery and kindergarten, discovered their surroundings through play, sensory exploration and the observation of endemic and migratory birds, such as the Juan Fernández firecrown and the shearwater.


From first grade through the final year of high school, students progressed through hands-on units that turned the island into a living laboratory. They explored the rocky intertidal zone, the water cycle in the Biosphere Reserve, seabirds, food webs, currents, algae and endemism. They also studied the archipelago’s marine culture, ocean acidification caused by climate change and the role of Multiple-Use Conservation Areas.


To ensure this learning would endure, Delta’s contribution equipped the schools with durable materials adapted to the island’s conditions: magnetic intertidal profiles, interactive maps of the archipelago and Cumberland Bay, and laboratory equipment. These were complemented by a Teacher’s Handbook created to serve as a local orientation guide for teachers arriving on the island.


The program also put people at its center. For one week, a team of three specialists, the same experts who co-designed the program, traveled to Robinson Crusoe Island. There, they trained teachers and supported them in the classroom and in the field to implement the project’s first pilot units with students.


### **An entire island learning**


The program’s reach was complete: it was offered free of charge to 100% of the municipality’s school enrollment. It directly benefited 256 people: 22 children from the Sandalito Kindergarten and Nursery, 169 students from Colegio Insular Robinson Crusoe and 65 teachers, education professionals, technicians and assistants, a significant contribution to public education on the island.


Its impact also extended beyond the school. Around 1,000 people in San Juan Bautista benefited indirectly, including families, artisanal fishers and tourism and diving operators. They took part through science fairs, exhibitions and citizen science projects that brought what was learned in the classroom to the rest of the community.


### **A collective effort**


The program was the result of a broad collaboration among local, academic and civil society organizations. Participants included the Mar de Juan Fernández Functional Community Organization; the Coastal Marine Research Station (ECIM) of the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, through its *Chile es Mar* project; Colegio Insular Robinson Crusoe; Sandalito Kindergarten; and Fondo Naturaleza Chile. Fundación Patagonia Azul channeled Delta’s funding to address the operational and logistical challenges of working on an oceanic island in one of the most remote areas of Chilean territory.


### **A legacy that stays on the island**


“Juan Fernández is close to having its entire exclusive economic zone protected, which will make it one of the largest marine protected areas on the planet, with nearly one million square kilometers under protection," said Cristian Laborda, Executive Director of Fundación Patagonia Azul. "For this level of protection to endure and be sustainable, we need to teach children from an early age. With this program, the ocean surrounding the island enters the classroom and becomes learning that stays in the territory, even when teachers change."


With the project concluded, everything that was built remained in the hands of the community. The materials, the Teacher’s Handbook and the skills developed among teachers now form a repository that the island itself manages independently. As a result, every new teacher who arrives on Robinson Crusoe has the tools to teach about the ocean that surrounds their students, and every child in the archipelago can grow up knowing the ocean their community chose to protect.


With this second phase, Delta and Fundación Patagonia Azul reinforced a shared conviction: ocean conservation is sustained over time when it is rooted in local communities and passed down from generation to generation. From Patagonia to Juan Fernández, the partnership added a new chapter to the same story: that of a Chile that sees the ocean as part of its identity and that, from the classrooms of Robinson Crusoe, has been shaping its next “Guardians of the Sea.”
